Full to bursting? 
 The Chinese buying wave is coming to an end, with the domestic market having 
moved into oversupply over the past month.  The question now is how much excess 
material China has agreed to take and how long it will take to work through the 
inventory.  The bottom may have been reached in consumption outside of China, 
but there are few signs that the recovery will be “V” shaped. 
 Supply has been continuing with few interruptions.  However, the oversupplied acid 
market remains a significant threat to smelter output. 
 LME prices are likely to face downward pressure, following the failure of a second 
attempt to breach $4,900/t in early May.  However, with China now oversupplied 
with copper units, a decline in price could be offset to a degree should the dollar 
weaken further.

Chinese wave breaks 
Since the last Monitor, there are clear signs emerging that China 
has finally sated its appetite for copper, with domestic refined 
cathode tightness easing.  SHFE copper prices have weakened 
as a result and the SHFE-LME differential has narrowed 
significantly in May.  In addition to record cathode imports in 
April of 317,947t, Chinese scrap buying appears to have run 
ahead of demand and released some of the pressure on the 
demand for cathode.  Prices offered for Japanese scrap are 
reported to be down some 30% from April and we have also 
heard that containers of scrap are not being unloaded at some 
Chinese ports.  Another reason for the easing of cathode 
demand is that domestic copper production continues to rise 
month-on-month, albeit at a slower rate than planned by 
smelters/refiners.  Additionally, rumours suggest that the SRB 
is selling 50,000t back to the market.  Whether the SRB is 
selling for a profit, because it lacks sufficient warehouse space or in a bid to buy the metal back at a later 
date at a lower price is open to debate. 
Chinese refined imports hit a new all time high in April.  At the same time, the differential (including VAT 
and duty) between the SHFE-LME has shrunk from an average of 23¢/lb in April to an average of just 9¢/lb 
as of 27th May.   The lag for delivery into China means that refined imports are likely to remain over 
300,000t in May and June but this trend will be unsustainable given rising domestic production and a 
narrowing arbitrage.  As a result, we anticipate a sharp drop in Chinese refined cathode imports from July. 
The surge of Chinese imports has seen LME inventory in Asian warehouses fall to only 1,950t as of 26 
May, with European stocks down to 92,750t and US to 222,425t.  Total LME cancelled warrants reached a 
high of 84,000t (21% of total metal) at the beginning of May.  Since then the pace of the draw down from 
the exchange has been rapid, especially of cancelled warrants in Europe as traders moved quickly to get 
material over to China to take advantage of the arbitrage.  However, the move in US warranted material 
came late in the day to catch the Chinese arbitrage window and we have heard that some of the material 
taken off warrant may have to be placed back on warrant, as the counterparty risk may be deemed too high.  
On the other hand, SHFE stocks slipped to 30,217t on 27 May, down 3,581t on the previous week 
registering a second successive decline.  However, given the growing domestic oversupply, this is likely to 
have been a temporary aberration and we expect exchange stocks to rise again in the first week of June. 
Prices stall below $4,900/t 
The rapid rally in copper prices stalled over the past month.  The 3-month price has traded in a wide range of 
$4,300-$4,850/tamid alternate bouts of short covering, long liquidation and the build up of new longs.  The 
volatility was driven more by the reaction to macroeconomic developments and persistently volatile dollar, 
rather than copper-specific factors.  Prices rose in early May, in line with stock markets based on hopes that 
the worst of the economic downturn was over, with the 3-month price touching a high of $4,845/t on 7th 
May.  The 3-month official price stood at $4,491/t at the end of April.  Prices then succumbed to selling 
pressure and traded down to a low of $4,323/t on 14th May, as the dollar strengthened on a rising risk 
appetite in the face of growing evidence that the economic downturn is close to the bottom.  Since then 
prices have moved higher with the 3-month official price rising to $4,655/t on 27th May.

The market had been in a steady cash to 3-month contango of just below $40/t from October 2008 until 
Easter.  The LME saw a short-covering rally after Easter, as those who were caught out by the jump in 
SHFE prices while the LME was closed scrambled to cover their positions.  This move saw the LME shift 
into backwardation, with the cash-to-three-month spread reaching a high of over $20/t by 30th April.  A 
cash-to-3-month contango has been re-established this month at around $15/t. 
Premiums ease in Asia and Europe 
With the closing of the SHFE/LME arbitrage window and the reduction in the level of cancelled warrants on 
the LME, premiums in Europe have eased to $50-60/t from the highs registered last month.  In the absence 
of Chinese trade, the focus will shift back to demand in Europe and the US, which is very low.  In the US, 
spot premiums remain low although they widened to 4.0-5.5¢/lb.  The top end of the range reflects delivery 
of very prompt material – particularly to scrap consumers who have not received delivery of their preferred 
feed.  In China itself, the import premium fell sharply to $135/t on average from the April peak of $200/t. 
There was only one Chilean tender concluded in the past month from ENAMI for a single 400t lot of AE 
LME branded material, for delivery in April.  The quotational period (QP) was one month after the date of 
shipment (although a QP of the month of shipment would also have been acceptable) and attracted a $147/t 
premium. 
Demand slump bottoming out… 
The main question facing the copper market now is how soon China will run down cathode stocks, as there 
is precious little support to month-on-month demand growth from the rest of the world, except South Korea 
and Taiwan.  The best that can be said is that demand outside of China may have hit bottom. 
In China, official semis production figures from the National Bureau of Statistics show semis 
production fell by 1.0% year-on-year in Q1 2009.  In addition, industrial production growth 
slowed to 7.3% year-on-year in April from 8.3% in March.  These signs of the fragile nature 
of the recovery in the country are supported by evidence from our China office, which has 
heard from semis producers in the country that orders in May are off considerably from levels 
achieved in March and April.  Meanwhile, external demand will not be of much help, as semis 
exports were flat month-on-month in April, while semis imports rose.  This is a clear signal 
that the sequential improving trend in Chinese trade seen since the lows hit in January has 
been broken.  All of the above strongly suggests that the early recovery in Chinese semis 
demand is very vulnerable to the higher copper prices.  However, in light of further research 
undertaken, we have upgraded our estimates of Chinese refined consumption on the back of 
lower scrap availability to year-on-year growth of 11.8% in Q1 and 11.5% in Q2. 
Outside of China the situation is much worse, with the latest data on semis production in Japan indicating 
that wire and cable shipments in April were down 26% year-on-year.  Although rolled output in the country 
rose by 29% month-on-month in April to 41,709t on a seasonally adjusted basis, this translates to a 49% 
decline in year-on-year terms.  This data confirms that seasonally stronger demand and some restocking, 
following the extreme destocking that took place in Q4 2008 and Q1 2009, is now feeding through.  
However, the sustainability of the rebound remains a big question mark, as industrial production is only just 
hitting bottom and the shape of the recovery is unlikely to be “V” shaped.  Demand in the US, Europe and 
Russia mirrors that in Japan and, with the summer holiday season only just around the corner, end-users of 
copper semis are reporting to semis producers that they will take extended holidays shutdowns in the months 
ahead.  These shutdowns are being driven by end users pessimistic prospects for the remainder of the year 
and their attempts to trim production volumes to match the expectation of this lower demand.

…but some of the rebound is partly 
borrowed from the future 
In Korea (see chart), there are similar signs to those seen in 
the rest of the industrialised world of a pick up in demand 
month-on-month.  However, the scale of the recovery in 
Korea is in part being “borrowed” from H2 2009.  Korean 
wire and cable production is being frontloaded this year and 
helps explain the strength of the recovery.  In particular, we 
have heard that the Korean national power utility had been 
encouraged by the government to frontload its’ spending to 
help support economic growth.  As a result, we understand 
that they will spend 68% of their total 2009 cable 
procurement budget in H1 2009, which in part explains the 
"early recovery" in copper consumption in the country.  In 
addition, North East Asia’s proximity to the relatively 
stronger Chinese market is benefiting semis exporters in both 
Korea and Taiwan.  However, with Chinese semis capacity 
continuing to grow, the sustainability of this is questionable. 
Sulphuric acid threatening smelter output plans 
There have been few market moving developments in copper production over the past month.  Prices above 
$4,000/t mean that most mines can operate profitably.  The main short run supply issues are mostly related 
to smelting and refining operations.  The current excess supply of sulphuric acid, in particular, is likely to 
result in further disruptions to smelter production.  In China, smelters have approached the government to 
introduce anti-dumping duties on sulphuric acid imports, which have ballooned from Japan to record levels 
of over 1Mt in the four months of the year.  At the same time, Chinese exports of acid have fallen to almost 
nothing.  Furthermore, the sulphuric acid market in China is likely to remain well over supplied, as several 
fertiliser plants are bringing on stream new sulphur burners that were ordered as a result of the high 
sulphuric acid prices seen over the last few years.  Therefore, the pressure on smelters to find a home for 
their acid will only increase, especially as the fertiliser season is peaking and demand for acid will begin to 
fall in the coming months.  A successful anti-dumping action in China would only pass the pain on to the 
Japanese smelters, so the question is one of where, not whether, new cutbacks will be announced, although 
timing will be difficult to gauge.  Other regions face a similar dilemma.  As for the one large net importing 
region, South America, it has insufficient infrastructure to take increased volumes of acid. 
Prices to come under pressure 
CRU has been bearish on copper prices for several months.  We estimate that the global Q1 surplus was 
579,000t and will fall to 367,000t in Q2.  Most of this is accounted for by a build up of off warrant stocks 
in China, both due to the estimated 300,000t of SRB stocking, restocking after the excessive destocking 
in Q4 2008 to the tune of some 100,000t and another 100,000t build up of working inventory at new or 
expanding refined cathode consuming semis plants. 
The closure of SHFE on 28 and 29 May means that there is a possibility for trading to be volatile those 
days.  However, as the LME has been generally taking direction from SHFE and wider economic events, 
the narrowing of the SHFE/LME arbitrage means we are just as likely to see sideways trading.  
Nevertheless, with China finally filling up with copper, the downward pressure on copper prices will 
mount over the next month.  This pressure from the fundamentals could be mitigated to a degree by any 
tangible signs of recovery in North America or Europe and, at least dollar denominated prices, by any 
further weakening of the US dollar.

Focus on Russia 
Domestic demand hit by economic downturn 
Almost all Russian domestic refined copper consumption is used for the production of wirerod.  CRU 
estimates that Q1 2009 wirerod production was down by 25% y-o-y to 125,000t as a result of weaker 
domestic and export demand.  After falling around 4% last year, Russian copper cable production has 
dropped by around 40% year-on-year in Q1 of this year, as both domestic and export markets have 
sharply contracted.   
The country’s cable industry is very pessimistic about the prospects for the rest of 2009.  The building 
wire, industrial and mining cable sectors have been particularly badly hit. Construction sector activity in 
Q1 was reportedly down by 60% y-o-y, whilst automotive production fell by 61% y-o-y in the first four 
months of 2009.  Industrial output fell by 16.9% y-o-y in April; for the period January-April, industrial 
output has fallen by 14.9% y-o-y. Since demand for electricity has fallen the utility sector is looking to 
delayed investment which inevitably impacts on power cable production.  Unlike in many other countries 
there is no sign of any significant government intervention that will directly boost cable demand.  The 
IMF has suggested that Russia’s GDP could fall by as much as 6% in 2009, reflecting lower industrial 
production as well as sharply lower commodity prices, on which the Russian economy is very reliant, 
along with restricted access to external financing and reduced external demand. 
Cathode exports rise as wirerod exports fall 
The lifting of export tariffs on copper cathode at the end 
of January, has boosted exports of cathode at the expense 
of wirerod.  Previously, Russian companies converted 
cathode into wirerod before exporting to avoid a 10% 
cathode export tariff.  Russian cathode exports were up 
113% y-o-y in Q1 to 111,200t, whilst wirerod exports fell 
by 55% to 47,7000t.  Traditionally, Russian wirerod 
exports have gone predominantly to USA, Europe 
(particularly Germany), the Gulf and North Africa.  The 
recent change in exports strongly suggests that Russian 
producers are reducing the amount of cathode that they 
convert into wirerod. 
Production falters 
Weaker demand and a shortage of scrap have contributed to a sharp fall in cathode production.  All three 
Russian producers cut back production last year, particularly in the fourth quarter.  These reductions have 
continued into Q1 2009 (see table below).  In Q1 2009, Norilsk Nickel reported that production by its 
Russian operations was 91,000t, down 8.3% y-o-y.  Production at Urals Metal and Mining Company 
(UMMC) was down 18.3% y-o-y, and at Russian Copper Company (RCC) it was down 38.1% y-o-y.

Norilsk Nickel has forecast that it will produce 290-305,000t of copper in 2009.  The Russian Copper 
Company plans to produce 80,800t at its Kyshtym plant in 2009. 
Financing has also been an issue for Russian producers, and the downturn has seen a review of 
investment plans.  Russian state-controlled bank VTB provided UMMC with a 4.8B rouble (US$174M) 
loan in November 2008.  This included 3.3B roubles to bolster working capital, repayable in one year, 
and 1.8B rouble for the refurbishment of the Sredneuralsk Copper Works.  The company has indicated 
that it may freeze new investment projects, though it intends to continue with those in progress.  RCC has 
also put on hold its investment programme for 2009. 
Scrap import tariff abolished 
In May, Russia abolished a 5% import tariff on copper scrap and waste for nine months to improve supply 
for domestic copper refineries.  Norilsk uses little scrap as feed, mostly sourcing concentrates from its 
own mines.  This has helped it maintain production better than the other Russian producers, RCC and 
UMMC, both of whom use a significant amount of scrap.  Around 47% of UMMC’s blister production 
feed came from low-grade copper scrap in 2008.

Industry News  
Production 
 
Grupo Mexico filed its own proposal for Asarco’s reorganisation in a Texas court, and therefore has 
formalised its US$1.55B bid for Asarco.  Subsequently, in mid-May, Grupo Mexico deposited 
US$1.3B in an escrow account to show the creditors that it has the cash. 
 
Harbinger Capital, a major Asarco bondholder, obtained permission from the US Bankruptcy Court 
to file a reorganisation plan for Asarco.  Harbinger Capital intends to submit a US$500M competing 
reorganisation plan for Asarco. 
 
A nine-day strike was held by 385 unionised workers at Xstrata’s Lomas Bayas mine in Chile as 
negotiations over pay increases between the parties failed to reach an agreement.  The union had 
asked for a 6.0% pay rise while the company had offered 3.7%.  There were also other non-resolved 
issues regarding bonuses and health and other benefits for workers.  The strike ended when workers 
accepted a proposal from the company.  In 2009, Lomas Bayas is expected to produce 67,000t of 
copper cathode. 
 
HudBay Minerals announced that it has closed the sale of its 16.7% share in Lundin Mining for 
C$236M (US$203M) to GMP Securitites.  HudBay Minerals will get cash relief and obtain some 
gains with this transaction. This stake was purchased in November 2008 as part of the bid by HudBay 
Minerals to takeover Lundin Mining. 
 
Southern Copper Corporation (SCC) said it expects to re-start operation at its Cananea mine in 
Mexico by the end of this year or the beginning of 2010.  Workers at Cananea started the strike in 
July 2007.  In April 2009 the government decided that the operator, Mexicana de Cananea S.A. (a 
subsidiary of SCC), was able to terminate its individual and collective labour agreements with unions 
and workers.  This decision is based on a force majeure declared by the government due to damage 
to machinery and equipment which has made it impossible to carry on mining activities at Cananea.   
 
Rio Tinto and China’s state-owned Chinalco obtained clearance from the Committee on Foreign 
Investment in the United States (CFIUS) regarding the proposed issue of convertible bonds to 
Chinalco and the indirect minority investment in Kennecott Utah Copper Corporation, as 
contemplated by the strategic transaction announced by both companies in February 2009.  
Meanwhile, shareholders in Rio Tinto have called for changes to the US$19.5B tie-up and it was 
reported that Chinalco plans to restructure the deal.  
Exploration and Development 
 
Antofagasta PLC announced that Minera Esperanza (70% owned by Antofagasta and 30% by 
Marubeni Corporation) has signed a definitive agreement securing a US$1,050M financing facility 
with a consortium of senior lenders for the development of the Esperanza copper-gold project in 
Chile.  The total investment on the project will be US$2,340M and is expected to start-up in Q4 2010 
with an annual production of 191,000t of copper in concentrates for the first 10 years. 
 
Vale S.A. has revised its capex expenditure for this year to US$9.035B from US$14.235B announced 
in October 2008.  The copper projects affected are: Salobo (US$375M from US$459M in 2009 of a 
total of US$1,152M) and Salobo expansion (US$6M from US$39M in 2009 of a total of 
US$855M).  Both projects are located in Brazil.  Salobo is expected to start-up in 2011 with a

late 2013 with an additional production of 127,000t/y of copper in concentrate. 
 
OZ Minerals announced that the results of its most recent exploration campaign have increased the 
resources of the West Copper deposit, which is located 800m west from Prominent Hill, by 32% to 
245,000t of contained copper. Prominent Hill is expected to produce some 85,000t of copper in 
concentrate this year and ramp up to 105,000t/y of copper in concentrate from 2010.  In Q1 2009, 
Prominent Hill produced 4,338t of copper in concentrate.  
Smelting and Refining 
 
In Zambia, Equinox Minerals announced on 6th May that its fully-owned subsidiary Lumwana 
Mining Company has signed a five year off-take agreement with Konkola Copper Mines.  The 
Lumwana mine will supply between 70,000dmt/y and 80,000dmt/y of copper concentrate, with an 
option of Lumwana providing additional quantities by mutual agreement under the same terms.  A 
previous off-take agreement with Mopani Copper Mines to supply its Mufulira Smelter with 
concentrates from Lumwana led to a dispute as Mopani and Glencore (majority owners of Mopani 
Copper Mines) claimed the concentrates did not meet the agreed technical specifications and refused 
to accept them.  Lumwana’s concentrates were then sold to the international market.  In 2009, CRU 
expects Lumwana to produce 150,000t of copper in concentrate. 
 
Jiangxi Copper announced it will resume full production at its operations in June after finishing 
repairs of an oxygen generator at its Guixi smelter.  In 2009, CRU expects Jiangxi to produce 
between 700,000t and 750,000t of refined copper. 
 
Two smelters in China have announced maintenance closures.  Jinlong Copper smelter started a 20-
day closure on 7th May.  In 2009, Jinlong is expected to produce 290,000t of copper blister.  Baiyin 
Nonferrous Co in Gansu province is due to close for maintenance in June, but is expected to produce 
80,000t of copper blister in 2009. 
 
The La Oroya smelter in Peru is unlikely to fulfil its environmental commitments in the scheduled 
period that ends in October 2009 and will therefore loose its operating license.  In 2006, its owner 
and operator, Doe Run Peru, received a 3-year extension from the government to complete the 
remaining US$193M out of US$500M of its environmental rehabilitation programme. Since March 
2009, Doe Run Peru has been facing problems to pay its suppliers who are mainly small and medium 
size mine operations in Peru.  Several mining companies that sell concentrates to Doe Run Peru 
agreed to give it a credit line of US$175M.  In addition, Doe Run Peru would have to fill a US$156M 
financial shortfall and pledge its shares to the Peruvian government as a way to ensure that it will 
fulfil its commitments.  La Oroya has already stopped all its circuits’ production except the copper 
circuit.  In 2009, La Oroya is expected to produce 38,000t of blister copper. 
Consumption 
 
Leading Japanese cablemakers Furukawa Electric, Hitachi Cable, Fujikura, SWCC Showa 
Holdings and Mitsubishi Cable Industries have all posted consolidated losses for FY2008.  Weak 
sales performance is attributed to the economic slowdown and the dramatic fall in copper prices 
during H2 2008.  Profits have also been hit by unfavourable copper inventory valuation due to the 
plunge in copper prices.

The Chinese government said that it would expand an existing subsidy program to encourage the 
purchase of new vehicles and home appliances, thereby boosting domestic spending.  China will now 
allocate CYN5B (US$733M) for owners of light trucks and passenger vans who upgrade to new 
models.  It also plans to spend CYN2B (US$293M) to fund discounts of new purchases of home 
appliances when customers turn in old goods, which will possibly give support to domestic copper 
demand.  The plan will apply to almost all household appliances, including air-conditioners, 
television sets, refrigerators, washing machines and computers.  Exports of these have been weak and 
the plan will help local producers to de-stock more quickly. 
 
KME Group announced that its copper and copper alloy semis output in Q1 2009 was down by 28% 
y-o-y to 113,700t.  The company attributed the sharp decline to weak demand due to the current 
gloomy economic conditions.  The product segment that has been worst hit is that of brass rod used 
in plumbing fixtures.  Consolidated sales revenues in Q1 2009 fell by 45% y-o-y to €459M 
(US$626M).  For the three months to March 2009 KME Group suffered consolidated pre-tax losses 
of €12.7M compared to profits of €7.5M realised in Q1 2008. 
 
According to preliminary data released by the Japan Copper and Brass Association, production of 
rolled copper and alloy semis in April fell by 48.6% y-o-y to an estimated 44,420t.  April was the 
ninth consecutive month that production fell, however, compared with March, the figure represents a 
28.7% rise.   
 
The Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association said that copper wire and cable sales 
in April dropped by 26.3% y-o-y and 18.8% m-o-m to an estimated 52,200t.  The deep economic 
downturn continues to take its toll on copper consumption in the world’s second largest economy.
